newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's Monster Raving Loonies prepare for power.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's Monster Raving Loonies prepare for power.

text.p: The shadow defence minister sweeps in wearing a flowing black cape and jester's horns, a skull dangling round his neck and a drooling Rottweiler dog at his side.
A burly man in eight-inch (20 cm) platform boots and studded leather body armour is huddled in furtive conversation in a corner with a party elder in a pink satin top hat and tail coat.
Britain's Monster Raving Loony Party is gathering for its annual conference, the last before a general election, and there is tension in the smoky air.
There are rumours of a cabinet reshuffle.
A Mahatma Gandhi lookalike shuffles to the bar, orders a pint of beer and nervously lights a cigarette.
Only the shadow chancellor of the exchequer wearing a "Save the Dodo" T-shirt, a red light winking atop his top hat, looks serene. He must have inside information.
Suddenly a buzz runs through the conference venue -- the bar of the Golden Lion hotel in the southwestern town of Ashburton.
The crowd parts and Screaming Lord Sutch, the Loonies' leader for the past 33 years, bounces to the microphone, his lurex tiger-striped suit glinting in the disco lights.
Sutch's sapphire blue eyes are a little puffy from his overnight trip and he is an hour late, but the party faithful are not disappointed.
There is a roar as Sutch predicts that the Loonies will have at least 200 members of parliament after the election, which must be held by next May.
"Go back to your constituencies and prepare for power," he commands his rapturous supporters, punching the air.

Sutch, 53, is perhaps a little optimistic. He and his party, with its motto "Vote for insanity - you know it makes sense," have taken part in 37 local and general elections since 1963 and have so far failed to win a single seat.
The Loonies had their biggest success in the northern town of Rotherham in 1994, when Sutch polled 1,114 votes.
The party says its own victory parties, held on the eve of elections, are partly to blame for its poor record.
Our supporters "wake up late with enormous hangovers and forget where the polling booths are until its all over," says the manifesto.

Add to this the fact that prisoners, the insane and members of the House of Lords (upper house of parliament) are not allowed to vote in Britain and the party claims that, by rights, it would have had a landslide in every election.
Undaunted, the Loonies have launched a manifesto brimming with vote-winning ideas such as plans to tow Britain 500 miles (800 km) south into the Atlantic to improve the climate.

If Sutch ever does win power, dogs will have to eat phosphorescent food to avoid the risk of people treading in dog mess at night and income tax will be incorporated into national lottery funds so everyone has a chance of winning their money back.
Nationalist Scots who want their own parliament will be able to borrow the London one, which will be put on wheels and towed around the country.

Boozy Britons won't have to go to work before lunchtime and their life will be made easier with the new decimalised time -- there will be 10 days to the week, 10 hours to the day, 10 minutes to the hour and 10 seconds to the minute.
"Current time-keeping is too confusing, especially when you're hung over and late for work," says the Loonies' manifesto.

While Britain's mainstream parties were holding their own annual conferences and struggling to stifle party splits that could threaten their chances at the election, there was an eerie unanimity among the Raving Loonies. Theirs is a party united around rock and roll and beer.

The Loonies would put rock and roll on the school curriculum and create universities where people could learn to be roadies. Sex and rock and roll would be available free from the National Health Service.
In keeping with his party's philosophy, Sutch makes his living as the lead singer of rock The Savages which, like his political career, has always teetered on the fringes of fame.
The Rolling Stones and the Sex Pistols have both played as support bands to The Savages and band members have included Keith Moon, the late drummer of The Who, and Jeff Beck of the Yardbirds.
"I'm going to be the first rock and roll prime minister," a confident Sutch told Reuters.
And the cabinet reshuffle?
Sutch glances out of the Golden Lion's grimy window.
"We'll have to wait until it stops raining before we take all that furniture out to shuffle it," he said.
